why:
D16, and the half of it that is not about Kotlin at all. The Java front-end has read JAX-RS since G6 and has never read Spring — the framework most Java services actually use. Adding Spring for Kotlin alone would have left that blind spot in the older front-end while claiming the graph understands JVM web services, so the reader lives in `pkg/jvm_routes.py` and both front-ends call it. This case and `kotlin/spring_routes` pin the *same* rules through two different grammars: Java spells an annotation `annotation`/`marker_annotation` with a `name` field and `element_value_pair` arguments, Kotlin nests a `user_type` or a `constructor_invocation`.

The Java-specific argument shapes are what this case adds. `method = {RequestMethod.PUT, RequestMethod.PATCH}` is an `element_value_array_initializer` naming **two** verbs, and two verbs on one method are two endpoints pointing at one handler — that is what Spring does, so that is what the graph says. `method = RequestMethod.POST` is the same argument written without braces. `path =` and `value =` are both accepted because Spring accepts both. A bare `@GetMapping` is a `marker_annotation` with no argument list at all and maps the class prefix itself.

`TopicClient` is the precision case: `@GetMapping` on an interface with no `@Controller`/`@RestController` is the Spring Cloud OpenFeign shape, where the annotation declares a route the service **calls**. It yields nothing. `anything` is the no-`ANY` rule: a verb-less `@RequestMapping` yields nothing rather than a verb the source never wrote.

refusals.why: PREDICTED BEFORE SCORING. `TopicClient` is a Feign-shaped interface: the same `@GetMapping` annotation, used to declare a route this service *calls*. Keying off the mapping annotation alone turns a consumer into a provider, and `pkg joins` would then pair a caller with itself. The class stereotype requirement is what prevents it, and it is the only thing that can.

PREDICTED BEFORE SCORING. A verb-less `@RequestMapping` matches every method. `ANY` is not a verb any client sends and no other front-end emits one, so such an endpoint could never join; expanding it to seven endpoints would invent six routes the source does not contain.

excluded: `TopicController.helper` carries no mapping annotation and yields nothing — the ordinary case, here to show that being a method of a controller is not by itself a route.

`produces = "application/json"` on `vets` is read past, not recorded: content negotiation is not part of an endpoint's identity in this vocabulary, and two endpoints differing only in `produces` would collide on one id anyway.

The six `java:org.springframework.*` import targets are external and stay out of the node ratio; the IMPORTS edges to them still count. `PageController` imports by wildcard as well, which names no single symbol and so adds no edge.

**Decided (was an open question).** A class-level `@RequestMapping` carrying a verb is read as a prefix only, and emits no endpoint for the class itself. It is legal and occasionally written, but no sample in the validation repositories does it, so there is no evidence either way — and the rule is left where a *missing* endpoint is the failure rather than an invented one. The expected set here is complete for the fixture as written.
